extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of mathematical logic (advanced undergraduates / graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive textbook-style exposition covering propositional logic, first-order logic, derivation systems, computability, and incompleteness, presenting definitions, theorems, proof sketches, and problems for teaching and learning formal logic and metatheory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive definition of wffs (Formula Definition 11A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set Frm(L0) of well-formed formulas is defined inductively: (1) every propositional variable pi is an atomic wff; (2) if α is a wff then ¬α is a wff; (3) if α and β are wffs then (α → β) is a wff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inductive definition constructs wffs in stages; any wff is built at some finite stage. The inductive presentation is the basis for proofs by induction on formulas and for the unique-readability/formation-sequence results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defined symbols as abbreviations (Definition 11B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defined (non-primitive) symbols are introduced as abbreviations: ⊤ abbreviates (α ∨ ¬α) for some fixed atomic wff α; ⊥ abbreviates (α ∧ ¬α); α ∨ β abbreviates ¬α → β; α ∧ β abbreviates ¬(α → ¬β); α ↔ β abbreviates (α → β) ∧ (β → α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined symbols are not primitive language elements but convenient abbreviations that shorten formulas and proofs; using more primitive symbols lengthens proofs and requires treating primitives separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic identity (Definition 11C)
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbol ≡ expresses syntactic identity between strings of symbols: α ≡ β iff α and β are strings of the same length containing the same symbol in each place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concatenation and substring relationships are expressed via ≡ (e.g., α ≡ (β ∨ γ) asserts α is exactly the concatenation of '(' , β, '∨', γ, ')').

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of induction on wffs (Theorem 12A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a property P holds for all atomic wffs and (1) whenever it holds for α it holds for ¬α, and (2) whenever it holds for α and β it holds for (α → β), then P holds for all wffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard structural induction principle for formulas; used repeatedly to prove properties like unique readability, balanced parentheses, and valuation facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced parentheses and no proper initial segment (Propositions 12B & 12C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any wff in Frm(L0) is balanced—has as many left parentheses as right ones—and no proper initial segment of a wff is itself a wff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These syntactic constraints follow from the inductive formation rules and are useful in parsing and uniqueness proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique Readability (Proposition 12D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every wff α has exactly one parsing as either (1) pn for some atomic pn, (2) ¬β for some wff β, or (3) (β → γ) for some wffs β and γ; moreover this parsing is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unique readability permits unambiguous induction on formula structure and justifies definitions (e.g., main operator of a formula). The proof uses induction on formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform substitution (Definition 12E)
rubrics_metrics.description: If α and β are wffs and pi is a propositional variable, then α[β/pi] denotes the result of replacing each occurrence of pi in α by β; similarly for simultaneous substitutions α[β1/p1, ..., βn/pn].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substitution is defined syntactically and is used both to build examples and to state meta-results about formulas and derivations (e.g., instances of schemas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation sequences as bottom-up construction (Definition 13A, Proposition 13C, Theorem 13E)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formation sequence ⟨α0,...,αn⟩ is a finite sequence of strings where each αi is either atomic or obtained from earlier αj, αk by ¬ or (→). Every wff has a formation sequence, and the set of strings with formation sequences equals Frm(L0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formation sequences give a constructive bottom-up view equivalent to the inductive definition; they permit proofs by ordinary induction on sequence length and show that formation rules are effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valuations and inductive evaluation (Definition 14A–B)
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuation v is a function v : At0 → {T, F}. The evaluation v(·) is defined inductively: v(pn)=v(pn); v(¬α)=T iff v(α)=F; v(α→β)=F iff v(α)=T and v(β)=F (truth-table clauses given).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semantics is truth-functional; valuation plus inductive evaluation determines the truth-value of any wff. Presenting clauses as truth tables clarifies intended connectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Determination of formula value (Theorem 14C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If valuations v1 and v2 agree on the propositional variables occurring in α, then v1 and v2 agree on α (i.e., v1(α)=v2(α)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes the locality of truth-functional semantics and is proved by induction on α; it underpins substitution and model-construction arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satisfaction relation and equivalence with evaluation (Definition 14D, Proposition 14E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satisfaction v ⊨ α is defined inductively (atomic: v(pi)=T; ¬β: v ⊭ β; (β→γ): v ⊭ β or v ⊨ γ). Proposition: v ⊨ α iff v(α)=T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satisfaction provides the semantic relation used to define entailment, tautology, and satisfiability; the equivalence with v(α)=T ties the relation to the evaluation function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic semantic notions and properties (Definition 15A, Proposition 15B–C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines satisfiable/unsatisfiable, tautology (⊨ α), contingent, entailment Γ ⊨ α, satisfiability of sets. Propositions: α tautology ⇔ ∅ ⊨ α; monotonicity (if Γ⊨α and Γ⊆Δ then Δ⊨α); transitivity; Γ⊨α ⇔ Γ∪{¬α} unsatisfiable; finite-satisfiability consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the standard semantic desiderata for propositional logic; the equivalences allow transforming entailment problems into satisfiability/refutation problems (basis for tableaux/compactness proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic Deduction Theorem (Theorem 15D)
rubrics_metrics.description: Γ ⊨ α→β iff Γ ∪ {α} ⊨ β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This links conditional validity to entailment with hypotheses and is used frequently when relating syntactic and semantic consequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for derivation systems: mechanical checkability, soundness, completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivation system is a purely syntactic method (finite syntactic objects) for establishing entailment and validity; it should be mechanically checkable. Desirable meta-properties: soundness (⊢α implies ⊨α) and completeness (⊨α implies ⊢α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soundness ensures syntactic proofs certify semantic truth; completeness ensures the proof system is strong enough to establish all semantic truths. Consistency notion should match satisfiability (consistency ⇔ satisfiable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic derivations (informal standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivations are sequences of wffs where each wff is either an axiom or follows from earlier wffs by inference rules; both axioms and inference steps must be mechanically checkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axiomatic systems are easy to describe and meta-theoretically convenient but produce derivations that are often hard to read and construct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequent calculus (§2.1) — structure and consistency criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequents are expressions Γ ⇒ Δ (pairs of sequences of sentences). Derivations are trees of sequents built from initial sequents by inference rules (e.g., ∧L, →R). Γ ⊢ α iff there is a derivation of Γ0 ⇒ α with Γ0 ⊆ Γ. A set Γ is inconsistent if some Γ0 ⇒ (empty right side) is derivable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequent rules manipulate left/right sides symmetrically; the calculus is systematic and useful for metatheory though derivations may be hard to interpret as ordinary proofs. Rules like weakening (WR) allow deriving arbitrary sentences from an inconsistent set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural deduction (§2.2) — introduction/elimination and discharge of assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural deduction gives each connective two rules (intro/elim). Proofs are trees whose leaves are assumptions; some rules discharge assumptions (e.g., →Intro discharges assumed antecedent). Γ ⊢ α iff there's a derivation whose undischarged assumptions are contained in Γ. Γ inconsistent iff Γ ⊢ ⊥.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural deduction models ordinary proof practice (conditional proof, proof by cases, indirect proof). Track discharged assumptions with labels; the undischarged assumptions at the root are the premises needed to derive the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tableaux method (refutation trees / signed formulas) — operational standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Tableaux operate with signed formulas (e.g., Tα, Fα) and build a refutation tree attempting to show unsatisfiability; rules decompose complex signed formulas into simpler ones until contradiction or open branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tableaux turn entailment into a systematic search for a counterexample valuation; they are often used as decision procedures for propositional logic and as proof-search tools in automated reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivability predicate / provability conditions (P1–P3) for arithmetical theories (Section 19.5–19.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a computably axiomatized theory T (e.g., PA) with a formula ProvT(y) representing provability, require: P1: If T ⊢ α then T ⊢ ProvT(⌜α⌝). P2: T ⊢ ProvT(⌜α → β⌝) → (ProvT(⌜α⌝) → ProvT(⌜β⌝)). P3: T ⊢ ProvT(⌜α⌝) → ProvT(⌜ProvT(⌜α⌝)⌝).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These derivability conditions are the formal requirements on the internal provability predicate needed to carry out Gödel-style and Löb-style metamathematics (e.g., proofs of the second incompleteness theorem and Löb's theorem). Showing P3 typically requires more arithmetical strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of theory consistency and the second incompleteness theorem (Theorem 196A/B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ConT as ¬ProvT(⌜0 = 1⌝). The second incompleteness theorem: for any consistent, axiomatized theory T extending Q with a provability predicate satisfying P1–P3, T does not prove ConT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a meta-theoretic constraint on what theories can prove about themselves; it depends on the chosen representation of ProvT but holds for any representation satisfying P1–P3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Löb's theorem (reflection principle constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: If T is an axiomatizable theory extending Q and ProvT(y) satisfies P1–P3, then if T proves ProvT(⌜α⌝) → α it must already prove α. Equivalently, instances of the reflection principle ProvT(⌜α⌝) → α are derivable in T only when α is derivable in T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Löb's theorem is proved via the fixed-point lemma and shows the limits of internal reflection; it is used to obtain short proofs of incompleteness results.
